title: The 1936 paper: Turing machines and the Entscheidungsproblem
text:
CHAPTER 3. TURING AND COMPUTABILITY
SECTION 3.1. THE 1936 PAPER: TURING MACHINES AND THE ENTSCHEIDUNGSPROBLEM

In Section 1.2 we left Hilbert's decision problem open: is there a mechanical procedure that decides, for any statement of first-order logic, whether it is valid? To answer "no," someone had to say precisely what a "mechanical procedure" is. In 1936 a 24-year-old Cambridge mathematician, Alan Turing, did this with an imaginary machine so simple that you could build it from a tape, a read/write head and a small table of rules. That imaginary machine became the standard definition of computation. Everything from the Z3 to a GPU running a large language model computes nothing that a Turing machine cannot compute in principle; they differ only in speed and memory.

1. Alan Turing

Alan Mathison Turing (1912-1954) studied mathematics at King's College, Cambridge, and was elected a Fellow of King's in 1935. In 1935 he attended lectures by the topologist Max Newman on the foundations of mathematics, which covered Goedel's results and Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem. Turing set out to answer the decision problem and wrote the paper "On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem," received by the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society in May 1936 and published in its volume for 1936-37 (a short correction followed in 1937).

Meanwhile, at Princeton, Alonzo Church had reached the same negative answer using his lambda calculus, in a paper published in 1936. When Newman learned of Church's work he supported publication of Turing's paper anyway, because Turing's approach was different and, many felt, more convincing about what "mechanical" means. Turing then went to Princeton, where he completed a PhD under Church in 1938. Later chapters follow Turing to Bletchley Park (Section 3.3), to computer design (Section 4.4) and to the 1950 paper on machine intelligence (Section 8.1).

2. The analysis: what does a human computer do?

Turing's paper is unusual because it does not just define a machine; it argues for the definition. He considered a person (in 1936 a "computer" meant a person who computes) working with paper and pencil following fixed rules, and he simplified the situation step by step:

  - The paper can be thought of as a one-dimensional tape divided into squares, each holding one symbol from a finite alphabet. Two-dimensional paper adds convenience, not power.
  - The person can only observe a bounded number of squares at once; we can reduce this to one square at a time.
  - The person's "state of mind" relevant to the calculation can take only finitely many forms, otherwise some would be too close together to distinguish.
  - In each step the person may change the observed symbol, move attention to a neighboring square, and change state of mind.

What remains is the Turing machine.

3. The machine

A Turing machine has:

  - a tape, infinite in one or both directions, divided into cells, each holding a symbol from a finite alphabet (including a blank symbol);
  - a head that reads and writes one cell at a time and moves left or right one cell per step;
  - a finite set of states, with a designated starting state (and, in modern formulations, one or more halting states);
  - a transition table, a finite set of rules of the form

        (current state, symbol read) -> (symbol to write, move L or R, next state)

At each step the machine looks up the rule for its current state and the symbol under the head, writes, moves and changes state. That is all. There is no arithmetic unit, no random-access memory, no instruction set beyond this table. (Turing's own notation used "m-configurations" for states and differed in small details; we use modern conventions.)

For an engineer, the closest everyday analogue is a finite-state machine (the kind you design with flip-flops and combinational logic, Section 2.1) attached to an unbounded external memory that it can only access sequentially, like a tape drive. The finite controller is the "processor"; the tape is the "memory."

4. A worked example: binary increment

Let us design a machine that adds 1 to a binary number written on the tape, with the head starting on the rightmost (least significant) digit. Alphabet {0, 1, B}, where B is blank.

    State "carry":
      read 1 -> write 0, move L, stay in "carry"     (1 + 1 = 0, carry 1)
      read 0 -> write 1, move L, go to "done"        (0 + 1 = 1, no carry)
      read B -> write 1, move L, go to "done"        (ran off the left end: new digit)
    State "done": halt.

Trace on input 1011 (11):

    1011, head on last 1, state carry
    -> 1010, head moves to third digit (1), carry
    -> 1000, head moves to second digit (0), carry
    -> 1100, state done. Halt.

Result 1100 = 12. Notice this is exactly the ripple carry of Section 2.2, executed sequentially by a single tiny controller instead of in parallel by n full adders. That trade of hardware for time is a theme of computer architecture: a serial machine with little hardware can do anything a parallel one can, only more slowly.

More complex machines are built the same way. Turing showed how to build up "skeleton tables," what we would now call subroutines or macros, for copying, comparing, searching for marked symbols and so on, so that longer computations could be described compactly.

5. Computable numbers

Turing's title speaks of computable numbers. He defined a real number to be computable if some machine, started on a blank tape, prints its binary (or decimal) digits one after another forever. The number pi is computable, since there are algorithms that produce its digits; so are sqrt(2), e, and every number you normally meet.

Turing's machines in this paper were designed to run forever printing digits, so the relevant notion of "good" machine was what he called circle-free: a machine that keeps printing digits indefinitely, rather than getting stuck in a loop where it prints no more digits. Keep this in mind: the modern "halting problem" is a reformulation of Turing's argument, not the exact form in his paper (Section 3.2).

6. Machines as numbers

Every Turing machine is described by a finite table. Turing showed how to write any table as a finite string of symbols in a standard format, which he called a standard description, and then as a single integer, a description number. This is the same idea as Goedel numbering (Section 1.2), and it has two enormous consequences.

First, there are only countably many machines: you can list them as machine 1, machine 2, machine 3, ... in order of description number. Since there are uncountably many real numbers (Cantor's theorem), almost all real numbers are not computable. Most numbers cannot be printed by any machine.

Second, a machine's description is just data, so it can be written on the tape of another machine. That leads to the universal machine (Section 3.2) and, in engineering form, to the stored-program computer.

7. The diagonal argument: something no machine can compute

Turing then asked whether a machine could decide, given the description number of an arbitrary machine, whether that machine is circle-free. He showed that the answer is no, using a version of Cantor's diagonal argument. Here is the idea in simplified form.

Suppose there were a machine D that, given any description number, correctly says whether that machine is circle-free. List all circle-free machines in order: M1, M2, M3, ... Each Mn prints an infinite sequence of digits. Let digit(n, k) be the k-th digit printed by Mn.

Now consider the sequence whose n-th digit is digit(n, n), the diagonal. Turing considered a machine H that uses D to step through description numbers, skipping those that are not circle-free, and for the n-th circle-free machine simulates it until it prints its n-th digit, then prints that digit. If D existed, H would be circle-free and would therefore be on the list, say as machine number K. What does H do when it reaches its own number K? It would have to simulate itself up to its K-th digit, which requires its own K-th digit, and so on: H can never print that digit. So H is not circle-free after all, a contradiction. So no such D exists.

(The simpler and more famous version flips each diagonal digit, 0 to 1 and 1 to 0, producing a sequence that differs from every machine's output in at least one place, so it cannot be on the list, yet seems computable if D exists. Turing chose the slightly subtler construction above; both make the same point.)

The lesson: there are well-defined yes/no questions about machines that no machine can answer in general. This is undecidability.

8. Answering Hilbert

Finally, Turing connected his result to logic. He showed how to write, for any machine M, a formula of first-order logic that is provable if and only if M eventually prints a certain symbol (for instance, 0). If there were a general decision procedure for first-order logic, it could be turned into a machine that decides whether an arbitrary machine ever prints 0, and from there into a decider of the kind shown impossible in part 7. Therefore no decision procedure for first-order logic exists. The Entscheidungsproblem has a negative answer.

This answer is independent of how clever we are or how big our computers become. It is not that the decision problem is hard; it is impossible for any procedure that fits Turing's definition.

9. Church's lambda calculus and equivalence

Church's approach expressed computation as the definition and application of functions. In lambda calculus, everything is a function, written with the Greek letter lambda (we will write "\" in plain text). For example:

    \x. x          the identity function
    (\x. x x)      a function that applies its argument to itself

and numbers can be encoded as functions too ("Church numerals"). Computation is the repeated simplification of expressions by substitution.

In an appendix to his paper, Turing proved that the functions computable by his machines are the same as Church's lambda-definable functions. A third definition, the general recursive functions of Herbrand and Goedel, was also shown equivalent around the same time. When different, independently motivated definitions coincide, it strongly suggests they capture a real, natural concept. This is the basis for the Church-Turing thesis: every function that is effectively calculable by a mechanical procedure is computable by a Turing machine.

Lambda calculus has its own long legacy in this book. John McCarthy's LISP (Section 9.2), the main language of AI for decades, borrowed its "lambda" notation for functions, and modern functional programming languages descend from the same idea.

10. Why this matters for engineers and for AI

  Limits. Some problems are undecidable no matter what hardware you have. In practice, many questions about programs (will this code ever reach this line? are these two programs equivalent? does this program terminate on all inputs?) are undecidable in general, which is why compilers and verification tools rely on approximations and heuristics. Rice's theorem (1953) generalizes this: essentially every nontrivial question about what a program computes is undecidable.

  Universality. Despite its simplicity, the Turing machine can compute anything any computer can. This means that the question "can a machine think?" is, under the Church-Turing thesis, the question of whether thinking is a computable process. Turing himself made this connection explicit in 1950.

  Abstraction. The Turing machine separates what is computed from how. Relays, tubes, transistors and future technologies only change speed, cost and memory size. This abstraction is why the history of hardware (Chapters 2, 4, 5, 6) and the history of AI algorithms (Chapters 9 onward) can be told as one story.

  Complexity. The Turing machine also became the yardstick for measuring time and memory, leading in the 1960s and 1970s to complexity theory (P, NP, NP-completeness), which explains why many AI problems such as planning and logical satisfiability are hard even when decidable.

11. Summary

  - Turing's "On Computable Numbers" (received May 1936, published 1936-37) defined computation through an analysis of what a human computer does.
  - A Turing machine is a finite-state controller with an unbounded tape and a transition table (state, symbol) -> (write, move, next state).
  - Machines can be encoded as numbers, so there are countably many; most real numbers are uncomputable.
  - A diagonal argument shows no machine can decide whether an arbitrary machine is circle-free; reduction to logic shows the Entscheidungsproblem is unsolvable.
  - Church reached the same conclusion with lambda calculus; the definitions are equivalent, which supports the Church-Turing thesis.
